label: First two copy-phase steps of long (L>=8) sequences
explanation: Reset-gate unit 20 fires only in the copy phase, early on: at the step right after <DEL> (input = orig(0), output orig(1)) and the step after that (input orig(1), output orig(2)), and only in long sequences (L=8 or 9). It is strongest at recall_idx 1, where the previous input is <DEL> (71% of activation mass, the top activations reach about 1.0 of max there). It is weaker at recall_idx 2 (26% of mass) and fades by recall_idx 3. Activation is higher for L=9 than L=8. Equivalently it tracks a large number of outputs still to come (to_go 6-7). L=7 gives only weak firing at recall_idx 1, and L<=6 essentially never fires. Never active in the original phase or at the <DEL> step. Token identity has little effect (a mild rise with repeated tokens and digits). A small tail of weak activations appears at the last copy steps of L=9 sequences.

issues: The L=8, recall_idx=2 cell is only about 51% precise (dev) and accounts for most of the false positives. Simple token variables don't split it: n_digits, in_count and digit vs letter input all give precision between 0.51 and 0.57. The explanation does say this step is weaker, but it is essentially a coin flip.
The claimed 'mild rise with more digits' does not show up in the L=8 recall_idx=2 cell (n_digits>=2: 0.509 precision; n_digits==0: 0.516). It is a minor overclaim at most.
Misses on test are scattered and small: 4.3% of activation mass, spread over L=7 recall_idx 1, recall_idx 3 and the last copy steps of L=9. All of these are mentioned in the explanation.

Confirmed claims: activation is never in the original or delimiter phases. recall_idx 1 holds 71% of the mass and recall_idx 2 holds 26%. L=9 is stronger than L=8 (recall_idx 1 precision 1.0 vs 0.95; mass 0.47 vs 0.23). L<=6 gives only 6 active steps. to_go 6-7 carries 89% of the mass.
Tried alternative: (recall_idx==1 & L>=8) | (recall_idx==2 & L==9). It has higher precision (0.945) but a lower test F1 (0.824), so the original predicate is better.
